content: Dysuria, or painful urination, may occur when methenamine mandelate is administered, particularly at doses higher than those recommended. This adverse effect can typically be managed by reducing the dosage and adjusting the level of urine acidification. However, in cases where urine acidification is contraindicated or cannot be achieved, such as with infections caused by certain urea-splitting bacteria, the use of methenamine mandelate is not advised. Methenamine mandelate should not be used concurrently with sulfamethizole, as formaldehyde, a byproduct of methenamine metabolism, reacts with sulfamethizole in acidic urine to form an insoluble precipitate. Formaldehyde, a metabolite of methenamine, can interfere with certain laboratory tests. It can cause falsely elevated results in fluorometric assays for urinary catecholamines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA). Additionally, formaldehyde can falsely lower urinary estriol levels when acid hydrolysis techniques are used, as it reacts with estriol. However, estriol measurements that rely on enzymatic hydrolysis are not affected by formaldehyde. Furthermore, formaldehyde can lead to falsely elevated 17-hydroxycorticosteroid levels when the Porter-Silber method is employed and falsely decreased 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) levels by inhibiting color development in nitrosonaphthol-based assays. Methenamine mandelate is classified as Pregnancy Category C. No animal reproduction studies have been conducted with this drug, and it is not known whether it can cause harm to a fetus or affect reproductive capacity when administered to a pregnant woman. Methenamine mandelate should only be prescribed during pregnancy if it is clearly necessary. Since its introduction, published reports on the use of methenamine mandelate in pregnant women have not demonstrated an increased risk of fetal abnormalities associated with its use during pregnancy.
